## cards/card

A card, or a lorebook, as one shape whatever it arrived as.

Four things can turn up and three of them are the same data:

- **V1** — a flat object of the six original fields.
- **V2** — `{ spec: 'chara_card_v2', data: {...} }`, which added the lorebook,
  the alternate greetings, and the two prompt overrides.
- **V3** — the same wrapper under `chara_card_v3`, with `nickname`, the
  creation dates, assets, and `character_book` renamed to `lorebook`.
- **A lorebook on its own** — SillyTavern's World Info export, which is the
  book without a character around it, serialised the way ST holds it rather
  than the way the card spec wrote it down.

Everything downstream sees one shape, so the importer has no idea which of
these it was handed. What could not be understood is not dropped: the
original goes to the sidecar whole, and export merges over it.

## LoreEntry

A card, flattened.

Type: [Object][210]

### Properties

- `name` **[string][211]** The character's, and what `{{char}}` becomes
- `title` **[string][211]** What to call the folder: the nickname when there
  is one, because that is what the card is known by where people browse for
  it, and on a scenario card it has nothing to do with the character's name
- `description` **[string][211]**&#x20;
- `personality` **[string][211]**&#x20;
- `scenario` **[string][211]**&#x20;
- `examples` **[string][211]** `mes_example`
- `greetings` **[Array][212]<[string][211]>** `first_mes` first, then the alternates
- `systemPrompt` **[string][211]** Rare, usually an ST preset's scaffolding
- `rules` **[string][211]** `post_history_instructions`, which a chat on it
  sends after its author's note. See `withOriginal`.
- `tags` **[Array][212]<[string][211]>**&#x20;
- `creator` **[string][211]**&#x20;
- `lore` **[Array][212]<[LoreEntry][2]>**&#x20;
- `raw` **any** Exactly what arrived, for the sidecar
- `title` **[string][211]** `comment` or `name`; the memo ST shows in its list
- `content` **[string][211]**&#x20;
- `keys` **[Array][212]<[string][211]>**&#x20;
- `constant` **[boolean][213]** Always in context, rather than looked up

## CHARACTER_FIELDS

The fields that say "character" and could not say anything else. `name` is
not among them: a lorebook has one too, and it is the book's title.

## shapeOf

What a file holds, without trusting its extension.

Both a card and a lorebook arrive as `.json`, and a card also arrives inside
a `.png`. What tells them apart is what is in them: a card has a name and a
greeting, a book has entries and no character.

### Parameters

- `value` **any** Parsed JSON, or a card pulled out of a PNG

Returns **(`"card"` | `"lorebook"` | null)**&#x20;

## readCard

A card of any version, flattened.

### Parameters

- `value` **any** A V1, V2 or V3 card

Returns **Card**&#x20;

## readLorebook

A book of lore, however it was serialised.

A card's `character_book` has `entries` as a list. ST's own export has it as
an object keyed by index, and each entry carries ST's field names beside the
spec's — `key` next to `keys`, `disable` next to `enabled`. Either way the
four things that matter are in there under one name or the other.

Entries with nothing in them are left out. ST's World Info is a flat list
with no headings, so a book with any structure to it is full of entries whose
whole job is to draw a line across somebody else's editor; they would import
as empty documents that say nothing to anyone.

### Parameters

- `value` **any** A `character_book`, a `lorebook`, or a World Info export

Returns **{name: [string][211], entries: [Array][212]<[LoreEntry][2]>, raw: any}**&#x20;

## entries

Type: [Array][212]<[LoreEntry][2]>

## uncomment

Take out what a card's author wrote for other people rather than the model.

`{{// …}}` is a comment: ST drops it before anything is sent, and authors
leave notes in it — "tweak this if…" — that were never meant to be read by
the model. The one macro where leaving it as written does harm. A comment on
a line of its own takes the line with it. The sidecar keeps them.

### Parameters

- `value` **[string][211]**&#x20;

Returns **[string][211]**&#x20;

## ORIGINAL

Where what a card overrides goes, as ST writes it.

## withOriginal

A chat's roleplay instructions with what they add to: its system prompt
after the profile's, its post-history instructions after its author's note.

After, unless they say `{{original}}`, which is where the other goes. That
much of ST's rule is kept, so a card that says where the writer's standing
instructions belong still puts them there. The rest of it, that a card's
instructions without the marker replace the writer's, is not: those are what
the writer chose and can see in the chat's settings, and a card that silently
dropped them would drop the Roleplay note's rules of play with them.

Resolved for each turn, so the chat keeps the card's text as the card wrote
it and the profile's part is whatever the profile says now.

### Parameters

- `value` **([string][211] | null | [undefined][214])** The chat's roleplay text, if any
- `original` **([string][211] | null | [undefined][214])?** What it adds to (optional, default `''`)

Returns **[string][211]** What the turn sends

## undecorate

Titles arrive decorated — `═══════[World]═══════`, `[☰] The Realm [☰]`,
`[📆]────↓Festivals↓────[📆]` — because World Info is a flat list and drawing a
box is the only way an author has to suggest a heading.

The decoration comes off and the name stays. What is stripped is punctuation
and symbols at either end; letters, digits and the spaces between them are
untouched, so a title that is only decoration keeps whatever it had rather
than becoming empty.

### Parameters

- `title` **[string][211]**&#x20;

Returns **[string][211]**&#x20;

## KEEP_AT_END

What ends a title rather than decorating it.

## stripEnds

Runs of decoration at either end: box drawing, arrows, dashes, spaces.

### Parameters

- `value` &#x20;

## stripEmptyGroups

A bracketed group with no letter or digit in it — `[☰]`, `[📆]`, `[›]` — at
either end. An author drawing a heading in a list that has none.

### Parameters

- `value` &#x20;

## unwrap

Brackets around the whole title, and only those. `[World]` is a box somebody
drew; `Tiger (Wild, Wild Pussycats)` is a name, and the difference is
whether the opener's own match is the last character.

### Parameters

- `value` &#x20;

## cards/chat

A card folder read back out of the tree, for starting a chat on.

Import and "Chat with…" are not the same moment. A card is imported once and
played weeks later, by which time the file it came from is gone and the
writer has renamed half of it. So nothing is remembered from the import:
what a chat needs is worked out from the documents, by their `kind`.

That is what `kind` is for. The titles belong to the writer — rename
`Description` to `Who she is`, drag it into a subfolder, and this still
finds it.

Design: `.llm/character_cards_design.md`.

## Greeting

Type: [Object][210]

### Properties

- `title` **[string][211]** The card's, and the chat's
- `name` **[string][211]** The character's: what `{{char}}` becomes in a chat

- `hiddenIds` **[Array][212]<[string][211]>** What a chat on this card hides: the shelf the

- `shownIds` **[Array][212]<[string][211]>** What it shows under that: the card itself
- `greetings` **[Array][212]<[Greeting][31]>** In the card's own order; the first is its `first_mes`
- `rules` **[string][211]** The card's post-history instructions, as written,

- `systemPrompt` **[string][211]** What a chat on it sends after its profile's

- `id` **[string][211]**&#x20;

Who a card folder is: the character's name.

The one in the sidecar, which is the character's own, what `{{char}}` meant

## readCardChat

Read a card folder for everything starting a chat on it needs.

Everything under the folder, however deep, because the writer may have
tidied it into subfolders. Hidden documents are read here on purpose: the
post-history instructions and the system prompt are hidden precisely so they do not also arrive
through the project block, and this is the route they were hidden for.

## cards

Character cards and lorebooks, read into the project as
documents.

Cards are SillyTavern's — V1, V2 and V3, as PNG or JSON — and they come in
because the people who write them have already done, by hand and at volume,
the work of turning traits into behaviours. A good card is a page of example
dialogue rather than a page of adjectives.

- **png** - The card hidden in a PNG's text chunks
- **card** - A card or a book as one shape, whatever version it arrived as
- **write** - That shape, written into the project as documents
- **macros** - `{{char}}` and `{{user}}`, filled in for the chat that plays a card
- **chat** - A card folder read back out of the tree, for a chat to run on
- **transcript** - A SillyTavern chat file, read into a chat's worth of messages
- **library** - A card as the writer's library keeps it, outside any project:
  read from a file, described for browsing, and found by name or tag
- **thumbnail** - A small copy of a card's picture, for the library's grid
- **sources** - Where a card is downloaded from, given a link to its page on
  botbooru or Chub, or to the card itself

Reading is pure — `png`, `card`, `macros`, `transcript` and `library` touch no store — and
`write` is the one part that has the tree in its hands.

Design: `.llm/character_cards_design.md`, and `.llm/card_library_design.md`
for the library.

### Examples

```javascript
import { cardFromPng } from '@/cards/png.js'
import { shapeOf, readCard } from '@/cards/card.js'
import { writeCard } from '@/cards/write.js'

const value = cardFromPng(await file.arrayBuffer())
if (shapeOf(value) === 'card') await writeCard(storyId, readCard(value))
```

## cards

Type: const

## cards/library

A card as the writer's library keeps it: read from a file,
described for browsing, and found again by name or tag.

The library holds cards as cards, outside any project. What it shows in its
grid, searches and sorts by is a lean description made here when a card is
added; the card itself is kept beside that as it arrived, for showing in
full and for writing into a project the way an imported file is.

Pure: nothing here touches a store. Design: `.llm/card_library_design.md`.

## cards/macros

`{{char}}` and `{{user}}`, filled in for the chat that plays a
card.

A card's documents say what the card says, macros and all. They are the card,
and a writer building one or changing one works with the macros the way every
other card tool does. What a macro becomes belongs to the chat: the
character's name, and the name the writer gave when they started it. So it
is filled in between the documents and that chat's model — in what its tools
read, the project block, the prompt and the author's note — and nowhere else.

Only a chat with names fills anything in. A chat on the Default profile,
where the writer works on the card, has none, and reads and writes the
macros as they are.

Nothing goes back the other way. What the model writes in a chat that fills
names in is written as it wrote it: a chat that plays a card is for play,
and in play a name is a name. `storedPassage` only finds where a passage the
model quoted is in the document.

Case and inner spacing vary between authors, and both are accepted. Nothing
else is: `{{date}}`, `{{random::…}}`, `{{roll:d20}}` and the rest are left
for the model to read, which says what they are for better than a value
frozen when the chat started would.

## MACRO

The two macros a chat has names for.

## Names

What the macros become in one chat. Either can be empty: a macro with no
name to become is left as it is.

Type: [Object][210]

### Properties

- `char` **[string][211]** What `{{char}}` becomes: the character's name
- `user` **[string][211]** What `{{user}}` becomes: the writer's, in this chat

## namesOf

The names a chat fills its macros in with, or null for a chat that reads
them as written.

### Parameters

- `chat` &#x20;

Returns **([Names][97] | null)**&#x20;

## nameFor

### Parameters

- `which` **[string][211]** `char` or `user`, in any case
- `names` **[Names][97]**&#x20;

## storedPassage

A passage the model quoted from the filled text, as the document stores it.

The model reads names where the document has macros, so the passage it
quotes to `edit_document` is not in the document as written. This finds it
in the filled text and gives back the stretch of the document that reads
as it. Where the passage starts or ends partway through a name, the stretch
takes the whole macro, and the replacement the part of the name the model
left out, so that what the document says afterwards is what the model asked
for.

Counted in the filled text, which is the one the model can see: a passage
that is there twice once the names are in is a quote that says too little,
even where the document spells the two differently.

### Parameters

- `text` **[string][211]** The document as stored
- `names` **[Names][97]**&#x20;
- `passage` **[string][211]** As the model quoted it
- `replacement` **[string][211]** What it should read instead

Returns **{count: [number][216], old: [string][211], new: [string][211]}** The passage and its
replacement as they apply to the stored text, when the count is one

## spans

Each macro filled in: where it is in `text`, and where its name is in `filled`.

## match

Type: [number][216]

##

Type: [number][216]

## cards/png

The card hidden in a PNG.

A character card is an image with its JSON base64-encoded into a text chunk
beside the pixels, so that one file is both the portrait people browse and
the data an app reads. V1 and V2 put it under the keyword `chara`, V3 under
`ccv3`, and a V3 file usually carries both so that older apps still find
something — so `ccv3` wins when they disagree.

Walking the chunks by hand rather than with a PNG library: a chunk is a
length, a four-byte name, the bytes, and a checksum, and that is the whole of
what this needs. The pixels are never decoded.

## SIGNATURE

Every PNG opens with these eight bytes.

## KEYWORDS

Where a card can be, best first.

## textChunks

The text chunks in a PNG, by keyword.

`tEXt` is Latin-1 and `iTXt` is UTF-8 with a compression flag and language
tags in front of the value; both are used in the wild for this. A compressed
`iTXt` is skipped rather than inflated — no card writer produces one, and
carrying an inflate for a case nobody has met is a cost with no reader.

### Parameters

- `data` **([ArrayBuffer][219] | [Uint8Array][220])** The file

Returns **[Map][217]<[string][211], [string][211]>** Keyword to its text

## chunks

Type: [Map][217]<[string][211], [string][211]>

## cardFromPng

The card in a PNG, still in whatever spec version it was written for.

### Parameters

- `data` **([ArrayBuffer][219] | [Uint8Array][220])** The file

Returns **(any | null)** The parsed card, or null if the image carries none

## decodeBase64

Base64 to a string, as UTF-8.

`atob` gives one byte per character, which is Latin-1 — and card text is
full of em dashes and smart quotes that would arrive as mojibake. The bytes
go back through a UTF-8 decoder to come out as what was written.

### Parameters

- `value` **[string][211]**&#x20;

Returns **[string][211]**&#x20;

## latin1

Bytes as Latin-1, a slice at a time.

Spreading the array into `fromCharCode` is the obvious way and overflows the
stack: a card's base64 runs to hundreds of kilobytes once its lorebook is in
it, and that many arguments is past what an engine will take. The limit is
on the call, not on the string, so slices of it cost nothing.

### Parameters

- `bytes` **[Uint8Array][220]**&#x20;

Returns **[string][211]**&#x20;

## cards/sources

Where a card is downloaded from, given the link someone has
to it.

The sites that share cards link to a page about the card, not to the card.
Each keeps the card as a file at an address that follows from the page's,
so the page's link is read for that address:

- **botbooru** - `botbooru.com/character/12345`, or its download link,
  becomes `botbooru.com/download/png/12345`
- **Chub** - `chub.ai/characters/creator/name`, or `creator/name` alone,
  becomes the card's PNG on `avatars.charhub.io`
- **Anything else** - a link straight to a PNG or JSON card, used as it is

Pure: nothing here fetches. Design: `.llm/card_library_design.md`.

## cards/thumbnail

A small copy of a card's picture, for the library's grid.

Card art is often a megabyte or more at full size, and a grid of a few
hundred of them decoded at once is a lot of memory for pictures shown an
inch wide. So each gets a copy the width of a cell on a dense screen, made
once and kept.

## THUMBNAIL_WIDTH

Wide enough for a grid cell at twice its size.

Type: [number][216]

## makeThumbnail

A copy of the picture at most `width` wide, or null where it cannot be
made: a picture that does not decode, or nowhere to draw it.

Opaque pictures become JPEG, which is small; a picture with transparency in
it becomes WebP, or PNG where the browser cannot write WebP, so its edges
do not come out black.

### Parameters

- `image` **[Blob][218]**&#x20;
- `width` **[number][216]?** (optional, default `THUMBNAIL_WIDTH`)

Returns **[Promise][215]<([Blob][218] | null)>**&#x20;

## cards/transcript

A SillyTavern chat file, read into a chat's worth of messages.

The file is JSON Lines: a header, then one message a line. It is a
transcript and nothing else — who said what, when, and what else they might
have said. Everything that made the conversation go the way it did lived
somewhere else in SillyTavern and is not in here: the card, the persona, the
preset, the lorebook. So a transcript says who it was with by name only, and
finding that character in the project is the caller's to do; see
`useCardChat().attach`.

Reading is pure. What comes back is rows in the shape `useChats().importChat`
already takes from a chat file of the app's own, so an ST chat joins a
project by the same road.

Design: `.llm/character_cards_design.md`.

- `messages` **[Array][212]\<Message>** In order, under placeholder ids: an import
  gives everything fresh ones

Whether this text is an ST chat, without trusting the file's extension.

The first line decides. A chat file of the app's own is one JSON document,
and its first line is either a lone brace or the whole envelope, neither of

One line of the file as a message.

`is_system` is not a role. It is ST's flag for a message the writer hid from
the prompt, and there is nothing here to hide one with; it comes in as what
it was before it was hidden, because a conversation with holes in it is worse
than one the writer has to trim.

The Author's Note, when the chat was sending one.

Despite the name it is not a note to self: ST inserts it into the prompt, a

sent, so it is not carried either.

## when

When something happened, from any of the ways ST has written that down.

Milliseconds first, then `July 19, 2023 2:05pm`, then the stamp it also
puts in file names (a date, an at-sign, and `14h 05m 33s 123ms`), then ISO.
The two in the middle are parsed by hand: what a browser makes of a date
that is not ISO is the browser's business, and this runs in more than one.

### Parameters

- `value` **any**&#x20;

Returns **([number][216] | null)** Null when it says nothing this can read

## titleFrom

A title from the file's name, which is `Elara - 2026-01-05@21h14m03s512ms`
until the writer renames it and `… - Branch #4` once they have branched.
The stamp says when the chat was started, which the messages say already.

### Parameters

- `filename` **[string][211]**&#x20;

Returns **[string][211]**&#x20;

## cards/write

A card, written into the project as documents.

The half of the import that touches the tree. What arrives is already one
shape whatever file it came out of — see `./card.js` — so this has no idea
which version it is writing, and a lorebook on its own is the same code with
the character half not running.

A card is a folder of ordinary documents rather than one blob, because a blob
is invisible to search, uneditable in the editor, and would need a viewer of
its own. As documents, every tool the app already has works on it, and the
question of how to edit a card answers itself.

They say what the card says, `{{char}}` and `{{user}}` and all, and are
plain: edited as the text they are and stored as written, which is the form
a card is written in everywhere else. A chat that plays the card fills the
names in for its model; see `./macros.js`.

Design: `.llm/character_cards_design.md`.

## writeMarkdown

Write a markdown file in as one document.

The plainest import there is, and the reason "Import" is not "Import a card":
a file of prose is a document, and the tree is made of documents. Titled
after the file rather than after a heading inside it — a heading is the
writer's text and eating it to make a name is a decision the importer has no
business taking. One too long for the editor to lay out comes in plain, as
the text it is: see editor/size.

### Parameters

- `storyId` **[string][211]**&#x20;
- `title` **[string][211]**&#x20;
- `content` **[string][211]**&#x20;
- `options` **[Object][210]?** (optional, default `{}`)
  - `options.parentId` **[string][211]?**&#x20;
  - `options.drive` &#x20;

Returns **[Promise][215]<[Written][175]>**&#x20;

## writeLorebook

Write a lorebook that arrived on its own.

A world several characters are played in, rather than one character's notes.
The same documents, with no card around them.

### Parameters

- `storyId` **[string][211]**&#x20;
- `book` **{name: [string][211], entries: [Array][212]<[LoreEntry][2]>, raw: any}**&#x20;
- `options` **[Object][210]?** (optional, default `{}`)
  - `options.parentId` **[string][211]?**&#x20;
  - `options.title` **[string][211]?** Overrides the book's own name

Returns **[Promise][215]<[Written][175]>**&#x20;

## writeLore

The entries, one document each.

Under a `Lore` folder of its own when this is a card, because a character's
own documents and the world's background are two different things to look
at. A book that arrived alone is already in its folder and goes straight in.

Keys go on the first line of the body rather than in the summary. The summary
rides in the project block on every turn, so what goes in it is paid for by
every turn of every chat for the life of the project; a body is paid for once
by a turn that opens the document. A key list is long, mostly inflections,
and earns nothing on a turn that is not looking for that entry — and in the
body `search_documents` still matches it, since that reads titles and
content.

The summary is left empty. It should be a sentence about what the entry says,
and writing that needs a model; an importer inventing one would be putting
words in the entry's mouth.

### Parameters

- `store` &#x20;
- `storyId` **[string][211]**&#x20;
- `folderId` **[string][211]** The card's folder, or the book's own
- `entries` **[Array][212]<[LoreEntry][2]>**&#x20;
- `$4` **[Object][210]** (optional, default `{}`)
  - `$4.into` &#x20;

Returns **{pinnedIds: [Array][212]<[string][211]>, documents: [number][216]}**&#x20;

## writeSidecar

The card exactly as it arrived, kept so an export loses nothing.

`hidden`, which already means kept from the model and out of reach of its
tools, and `plain` so it is stored as written rather than settled to what the
editor can show. It still appears in the tree, dimmed — the writer can see
what the import wrote, open it, and delete it. A sidecar nobody can find is a
file that rots.

### Parameters

- `store` &#x20;
- `storyId` **[string][211]**&#x20;
- `folderId` **[string][211]**&#x20;
- `raw` **any**&#x20;

Returns **[number][216]** How many documents this wrote

`Cards/Characters` and `Cards/Lorebooks`, so that a character imported later

can be played in, lands somewhere nobody hides by default. Under `Cards/`
so that a novel's own `Characters` folder is never the one hidden.
